sense: give oneself or one’s time to

terms.gloss: give up; with sē, devote oneself to
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation; sē dēdere + dative
evidence: Cic. Q. fr. 3.5.4: sē litterīs (Lewis & Short)
Cic. de Or. 1.10: sē penitus mūsicīs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Cicero’s usual turn: sē litterīs, studiīs, alicui tōtum dēdere. The participle dēditus is “devoted to, given over to”. Its first sense is to give up, hand over, and of a city or army to surrender (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: throw oneself into, apply oneself to
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation; in or ad + accusative, or dative
evidence: Cic. de Or. 1.34: in aliquod studium (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally to lean or lie on something; of effort, to bend all one’s attention to a task (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: give one’s attention or effort to
evidence: Cic. Fam. 13.11.1: operam dare, ut nē quid meōrum tibi esset ignōtum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The everyday phrase for spending one’s effort on something; with ut, to take care that.

terms.gloss: vow to a god; devote to death
terms.comment: Not the everyday word: chiefly to vow something to a god, or oneself to death for one’s country, as the Decii did; only rarely “devote oneself to” a person or cause (Caes. BG 3.22.2) (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: devote oneself to, give oneself up to

phrases.english: given over to sleep and food
to which (our country) we ought to devote ourselves entirely
